title: Arrivals
teaches: Species carried to new places, and the few that take over

blocks.text: In 1958 the Oxford ecologist Charles Elton, who had worked out food chains and pyramids thirty years before, published a short book called *The Ecology of Invasions by Animals and Plants*. He opened it with three stories.

In 1904 a forester at the Bronx Zoo in New York noticed the American chestnut trees there dying of a canker, a spreading wound in the bark. The cause was a fungus from Asia, probably carried on imported nursery trees. Asian chestnuts had lived alongside it for ages and mostly survived; American chestnuts had never met it. Spreading on the wind, it killed nearly every chestnut across the eastern forests within about forty years, billions of trees that had made up a quarter of the canopy in places[^chestnut].

In 1905 a landowner near Prague released five muskrats, brought from North America for their fur. Within fifty years their descendants had spread across central Europe, digging into the banks of rivers and fishponds, and Elton printed a map of their advance like a spreading stain. And in 1890 a New Yorker named Eugene Schieffelin released sixty European starlings in Central Park, then forty more the next year. There are now tens of millions of starlings in North America, from Mexico to Alaska[^starling].

Elton's stories are famous because they are unusual. Schieffelin belonged to a society that set out to release European birds in America, and in the late nineteenth century skylarks, song thrushes, nightingales, chaffinches and others were let go in American parks. Nearly all of them died out. The starling and the house sparrow were the exceptions.

The same is true of species carried by accident in ballast water, on crates and in soil. The British ecologist Mark Williamson put it as a rough **tens rule**: of the kinds that are brought to a new place, about one in ten is found living wild; of those, about one in ten settles in and breeds; and of those, about one in ten spreads and becomes a pest. The numbers vary a great deal, but the pattern holds[^tens]. A newcomer usually arrives in small numbers, in an unfamiliar place, and a few bad seasons finish it off, the way any small population can wink out by chance.

A few newcomers explode because they leave their enemies behind. At home, a plant or animal is held down by its predators, parasites and diseases, as lesson 7's sea stars held down the mussels. A few founders carried across an ocean rarely bring all of these with them. In 2003 Mark Torchin and colleagues compared animals in their home ranges and where they had been introduced, and found that the introduced populations carried about half as many kinds of parasite, and were less heavily infected by those they had.

blocks.caption: Twenty releases of the same newcomer, each starting with the same number of animals. Each year brings good luck or bad; the enemies of its old home slow its growth. A model.
blocks.task: Release it with and without its enemies, and find releases that take over

blocks.text: The model shows both halves of the story. With its enemies, almost every release fizzles out or hangs on in small numbers. Without them, most take off, yet a release of only a few animals still often dies out before it can grow. That is one reason a species released many times, or arriving again and again in cargo, is more likely to take hold.

Two other things help a newcomer. One is a way of living that nothing in the new place already fills. Guam, in the western Pacific, had no snakes, apart from a tiny blind burrower, when the brown tree snake arrived from the New Guinea region, probably in military cargo after the Second World War. The island's birds had no defence against a predator that climbs trees at night. By the 1980s most of Guam's native forest birds had disappeared[^guam].

The other is disturbance. Roadsides, ploughed fields, burned ground and building sites are open to whatever seeds land first, and the weeds of the world are mostly plants that thrive on broken ground. Many invaders are most common where people have already changed the land, and it is often hard to say whether the newcomer caused the change or only took advantage of it. Cheatgrass, an annual grass that arrived in eastern Washington in grain shipments, does both, and the branch on the dry side of the state follows it.

If escaping enemies helps an invader, bringing one of them over might hold it down. This is called **biological control**. Purple loosestrife, a tall magenta-flowered plant from Europe, spread through the wetlands of North America in the twentieth century, including Washington's. In the 1990s, after years of testing that they would eat nothing else, two European leaf beetles that feed on loosestrife were released. In many wetlands, including some in Washington, they have cut the loosestrife back sharply.

Biological control has also gone badly wrong. The cane toad, released in Australia in 1935 to eat beetles in sugar cane, barely touched the beetles and spread across the north of the continent, poisoning the native predators that tried to eat it. The difference lay in testing: the loosestrife beetles were tested for years on dozens of other plants; the toad, which will eat almost anything, never could have passed.

blocks.caption: Purple loosestrife in a wetland at Concord, Massachusetts: a European plant that spread across North America.

blocks.title: Outside
points: Walk a city park or a roadside and count the plants you know came from elsewhere: Himalayan blackberry, English ivy, Scotch broom, dandelions. Then find a patch of land nobody has dug or mown for many years and count again. The disturbed ground will usually hold far more newcomers.

blocks.caption: Five questions on newcomers
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What usually happens to a species released in a new place?
choices: It dies out, often before anyone notices
It spreads and becomes a pest
It replaces a native species of the same kind
items.why: Most of the European birds released in America died out. The starling was the exception, which is why it is remembered.

items.ask: Why did chestnut blight kill American chestnuts but not Asian ones?
choices: The American trees had never met the fungus and had no defence
The fungus grows only in American soils
Asian chestnuts grow too far apart to catch it
items.why: Asian chestnuts had lived with the fungus for ages and resisted it. American trees had no such history with it.

items.ask: What did Torchin and colleagues find about introduced animals?
choices: They carried about half as many kinds of parasite as at home
They carried more parasites, picked up on the journey
They had the same parasites in both places
items.why: Founders leave many of their enemies behind, one reason a few newcomers grow so fast.

items.ask: In the figure, freed of its enemies, why does a release of only a few animals still often die out?
choices: A few bad years in a row can finish off a small population by chance
Small groups can't find the food
items.why: Chance hits small populations hardest. More founders, or repeated arrivals, make success likelier.

items.ask: Why did the loosestrife beetles work when the cane toad failed?
choices: The beetles were tested to make sure they ate only loosestrife
Loosestrife grows only in wet places the toads avoid
The beetles were released in far greater numbers
items.why: A control agent that eats only its target can't turn on other species. The toad would eat anything.

summary: **Elton opened the study of invasions in 1958.** Chestnut blight, muskrats in Europe and starlings in Central Park were his examples.
**Most arrivals fail.** Williamson's rough tens rule: one in ten escapes, one in ten of those settles, one in ten of those spreads.
**Small founding groups die out by chance.** Many releases or repeated arrivals make success likelier.
**Newcomers often leave their enemies behind.** Introduced animals carry about half as many kinds of parasite as at home.
**Empty roles and broken ground help.** Guam's snake had no rivals; weeds thrive on disturbed land.
**Biological control brings an enemy over.** It worked for loosestrife after careful testing, and failed badly with the cane toad.

chestnut.title: The chestnut today
chestnut.text: The roots of many American chestnuts survived, and still send up shoots that grow a few metres before the blight kills them back. Breeders have crossed the tree with resistant Asian chestnuts, and others have added a wheat gene that disarms the fungus, hoping to bring it back to the forest.

starling.title: The Shakespeare story
starling.text: It is often said that Schieffelin wanted to bring every bird mentioned in Shakespeare to America. Historians have found no sign of this in writings from his time; the story seems to have been added decades later.

guam.title: A quiet forest
guam.text: With most of the birds gone, Guam's forests have fewer seeds carried away from parent trees and many more spiders, which the birds once ate. A few of the lost birds survive in captivity and on nearby snake-free islands.

tens.title: How rough the tens rule is
tens.text: Williamson and Fitter published the rule in 1996 from British plants and animals. Later studies found the steps for birds and mammals much less steep, often one in two rather than one in ten, since people choose to release animals that are likely to survive.
